explanations.answer: prophets
explanations.explanation: Prophets it is. Paul says God promised the gospel beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures. So the good news was written down long before Paul ever picked up a pen. Some of us can't plan a cookie batch an hour ahead, and this was promised way back.

explanations.answer: priests
explanations.explanation: I see why priests came to mind, since they're all over the Scriptures. But Paul says the gospel was promised beforehand through His prophets. Those are the ones God spoke through, and their words are in the Holy Scriptures. Paul says nothing about priests here, friend.

explanations.answer: judges
explanations.explanation: Judges is a solid guess if you've read a lot of Israel's history. Paul's word here is prophets, though. He says God promised the gospel beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures. Judges don't show up in this verse at all.

explanations.answer: David
explanations.explanation: David is the name Paul gives. He says God's Son was a descendant of David according to the flesh. That's the human side of the family line. Paul puts it right at the start of his letter, and I bet he wants Rome to hear it.

explanations.answer: Saul
explanations.explanation: Saul was a king of Israel (1 Samuel 11:15), so I get the mix-up. But Paul names someone else here. He says God's Son was a descendant of David according to the flesh. David, friend, not Saul.

explanations.answer: Ahab
explanations.explanation: Ahab was a king of Israel (1 Kings 16:29), so you're in the right neighborhood. Paul, though, says God's Son was a descendant of David according to the flesh. That's the name he writes. Ahab isn't the name Paul gives.

explanations.answer: By His resurrection from the dead
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Paul says that through the Spirit of holiness, Jesus was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead. Of everything Paul could have pointed to, he points there. Then he gives the name: Jesus Christ our Lord.

explanations.answer: By His miracles in Galilee
explanations.explanation: Miracles in Galilee is a fair guess, baker. But Paul's answer in this verse is different. He says Jesus was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead. That's the line to hold onto.

explanations.answer: By His teaching in the temple
explanations.explanation: Teaching in the temple is a good guess. But that's not what Paul writes in this verse. He says Jesus was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead. Paul keeps it to that one.

explanations.answer: To call the Gentiles to obedience from faith
explanations.explanation: Right on target. Paul says we received grace and apostleship to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith. Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. So the call goes out wide, and it's an obedience that comes from faith.

explanations.answer: To guard the Law of Moses in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: The Law of Moses is a big deal in Scripture. But Paul doesn't say that here. He says grace and apostleship were given to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith. Nothing about guarding anything in Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: To build a temple for the believers in Rome
explanations.explanation: A building project would be a fine thing to have on a to-do list. Paul's purpose in this verse is different, though. He says grace and apostleship were received to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith. No bricks, no blueprints.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True. Paul says to them, "And you also are among those who are called to belong to Jesus Christ." (Romans 1:6) He counts the believers in Rome right in with the called ones. You got it, baker.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: This one's actually true. Paul says to the believers in Rome, "And you also are among those who are called to belong to Jesus Christ." (Romans 1:6) He puts them right in with the called.

explanations.answer: God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul writes. Grace and peace come from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. He puts both names right there in his greeting. I'd take a letter that opens like that over a coupon flyer any day.

explanations.answer: The angels of God and the prophets
explanations.explanation: Angels and prophets do show up in Scripture a lot. But Paul doesn't name them here. He says grace and peace are from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Those are the two names in his greeting.

explanations.answer: The elders of the church in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Jerusalem comes up a lot in the Bible, so I see how it crept in. Paul's greeting names two sources, though. Grace and peace come from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. No elders are mentioned in this greeting.

explanations.answer: Their faith is being proclaimed all over the world
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says he thanks God for all of them because their faith is being proclaimed all over the world. News about their faith is traveling. Paul takes that and turns it into a thank-you to God.

explanations.answer: Their church is the largest one in the whole world
explanations.explanation: Paul never says anything about the size of their church. His reason is that their faith is being proclaimed all over the world. That's what he thanks God for. I'd say the headcount stays out of it.

explanations.answer: They sent money to pay for all his travels
explanations.explanation: Money doesn't come up in these verses. Paul gives one reason for his thanks: their faith is being proclaimed all over the world. That's the whole reason on the page, friend. No receipts needed.

explanations.answer: That by God's will he may come to Rome
explanations.explanation: That's his request. Paul says he's asking in his prayers at all times that now at last, by God's will, he may succeed in coming to them. He keeps bringing it to God. I think a man who prays that long for a visit really wants to get there.

explanations.answer: That Rome's rulers would turn to God
explanations.explanation: That's a big prayer, but it isn't the one Paul names here. He says he's asking that now at last, by God's will, he may succeed in coming to them. The prayer is about his visit.

explanations.answer: That the church would grow in number
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention numbers in this prayer. He says he's asking that now at last, by God's will, he may succeed in coming to them. That's the request on the page.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True. Paul says he and they may be "…mutually encouraged by each other’s faith." (Romans 1:12) So the encouragement goes both ways. It isn't just him encouraging them. You got it, baker.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: It's actually true. Paul says he and they may be "…mutually encouraged by each other’s faith." (Romans 1:12) The encouragement goes both ways, not just from him to them.

explanations.answer: He has been prevented until now
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's what Paul says. He planned to come to them often, but has been prevented from visiting until now. The text doesn't say what stopped him, so I won't guess. He just tells them he kept planning.

explanations.answer: The church asked him to wait
explanations.explanation: Paul never says the church asked him to wait. He says he often planned to come, but has been prevented from visiting until now. That's all the verse gives, friend.

explanations.answer: He wanted to finish in Spain first
explanations.explanation: Spain isn't in these verses. Paul says he often planned to come, but has been prevented from visiting until now. He doesn't give a reason, so I'll stick with what he wrote.

explanations.answer: eager
explanations.explanation: Eager is his word. Paul says he's obligated to Greeks and non-Greeks, to the wise and the foolish, and that's why he's so eager to preach the gospel to the believers in Rome too. I'm eager when a fresh batch comes out of the oven. Paul's eager about the gospel.

explanations.answer: afraid
explanations.explanation: I can see why afraid might come to mind, since Rome was a big place. Paul's word here is eager, though. He says that's why he's so eager to preach the gospel to them too. Fear isn't what he writes.

explanations.answer: slow
explanations.explanation: Slow is nearly the opposite of what Paul writes. He says he's so eager to preach the gospel to the believers in Rome too. He's leaning forward, not dragging his feet.

explanations.answer: It is the power of God for salvation
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says he isn't ashamed of the gospel because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. That's his reason, plain and simple. It's power that comes from God.

explanations.answer: It is the law of Moses for the Jews
explanations.explanation: The law of Moses is a big part of Scripture. But Paul doesn't say that here. He says he isn't ashamed of the gospel because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.

explanations.answer: It is the wisdom of the wise for all people
explanations.explanation: Paul does mention the wise a verse earlier, so I see the link. But his reason for not being ashamed is different. He says the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Paul actually says it's not only for the Jews. He says the gospel is the power of God for salvation "…to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek." (Romans 1:16) Everyone who believes is in.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: False is right. Paul says the gospel is the power of God for salvation "…to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek." (Romans 1:16) The word he uses is everyone.

explanations.answer: faith
explanations.explanation: Faith, from start to finish. Paul says the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish. Then he adds what is written: "The righteous will live by faith." That one word carries the whole verse.

explanations.answer: works
explanations.explanation: Works is a natural guess, because we're all used to earning things. But Paul says the righteousness of God comes by faith from start to finish. He backs that up with this: "The righteous will live by faith." Faith is the word he lands on.

explanations.answer: sacrifice
explanations.explanation: Sacrifice is a big word in Scripture, so I get why it came to mind. But here Paul says the righteousness of God comes by faith from start to finish. His quote says it too: "The righteous will live by faith." Faith is the one he picks.
